About the report
Principle of Reporting
The Financial Statements and statutory disclosures, such as 
the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report, Board’s Report, Management Discussion and Analysis (MD&A), and Corporate Governance Report, adhere to the requirements of the Companies Act, 2013, Indian Accounting Standards, SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, and Secretarial Standards issued by the Institute of Company Secretaries of India.
Assurance
To ensure the integrity of the numbers presented in the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report for FY26, a Reasonable and/or Limited Assurance Statement on key performance indicators (‘KPIs’), by SGS India Private Limited, is available on our website at www. industowers.com.
Management Responsibility Statement
The management of Indus acknowledges its responsibility for maintaining the integrity, transparency, and accuracy of the information presented in the Integrated Annual Report. The report strives to address business-critical material issues and communicates the organisation’s ability to pursue opportunities and mitigate risks.
GRI Content Index
GRI content index mapping for the Integrated Annual Report forms part of this report.
Forward-looking Statements
Some information in this report may contain forward-looking statements. We have based these forward-looking statements on our current beliefs, expectations, and intentions as to facts, actions, and events that will or may occur in the future. Such statements generally are identified by forward-looking words such as ‘believe,’ ‘plan,’ ‘anticipate,’ ‘continue,’ ‘estimate,’ ‘expect,’ ‘may,’ ‘will’ or other similar words. A forward-looking statement may include a statement of the assumptions or basis underlying such statement. We have chosen these assumptions or basis in good faith, and we believe that they are reasonable in all material respects. However, we caution you that forward-looking statements and assumed facts or bases almost always vary from actual results, and the differences between the results implied by the forward-looking statements and assumed facts or basis and actual results can be material, depending on the circumstances. You are requested to note that forward-looking statements are based on current assumptions and are relevant as on the date of this report. We do not commit to updating them despite future risks or uncertainties. Due to inherent risks and uncertainties, forward-looking statements may not materialise and should be read in conjunction with this supplemental disclosure.Scope of Reporting

Indus Towers is India’s leading 
provider of passive telecom infrastructure, enabling mobile and broadband connectivity at a national scale. We design, deploy, own and manage one of the world’s largest tower portfolios, supporting seamless network coverage for mobile network operators through a robust shared-infrastructure model. Our footprint spans all telecom circles, with a growing base of towers and related infrastructure, distributed solar footprint and next-gen solutions that underpin India’s digital expansion. 
We are advancing India’s digital ecosystem and shaping future connectivity. We offer end-to-end site solutions, from tower infrastructure to power management and uptime delivery, helping operators scale efficiently while reducing their capital intensity. Our commitment to sustainability, digital innovation and energy transition strengthens the resilience and efficiency of our portfolio.
Looking Ahead
We are well-positioned to support the next phase of India’s digital growth. We will continue to build on our leadership in telecom infrastructure while continuing to improve service quality, expand footprint, and operate responsibly.Mission

India’s digital infrastructure landscape continues to evolve rapidly, supported by sustained 
growth in data consumption, accelerating 5G adoption and increasing digitalisation across sectors. Against this backdrop, Indus Towers is well positioned to capitalise on the next phase of growth through its strong market position, deep customer relationships, extensive infrastructure portfolio and proven execution capabilities. Our continued focus on operational excellence, technology-led transformation, disciplined capital allocation and sustainable growth provides a strong foundation to create long-term value for all stakeholders.  
Driving sustainable scale 
with digital transformation and robust fundamentalsINVESTMENT CASE
India’s telecom sector is entering a fundamentally stronger growth phase, underpinned by 
increasing data consumption, potential for tariff improvement, improving financial metrics and sustained policy support. With continued investments in network expansion, 5G rollouts and data consumption, the telecom tower industry is expected to witness a sustained demand for passive infrastructure creation. Given Indus’ market leadership, it is well-placed to secure a substantial share of customer rollout activities and maintain its growth trajectory.Growth anchored in enterprise strength

Adjacency and expansion 
opportunities
Indus Towers is actively expanding into 
adjacent telecom infrastructure segments, including in-building solutions (IBS), to broaden its addressable market. Strong customer relationships and early engagement with developers and enterprises have enabled sustained momentum in IBS deployments across enterprise, institutional and public infrastructure segments, strengthening our position in indoor connectivity solutions.
IBS colocations (LTD)
~1.7K
We have also taken a strategic step towards 
international expansion through planned entry into Africa. Given the favourable growth outlook and visibility of anchor tenant demand, this initiative represents a compelling diversification opportunity and a long-term growth lever. We aim to leverage our core strengths – high-quality service delivery, reliable network operations and cost-efficient infrastructure – to establish a strong presence in these markets.
As part of this strategy, we have identified 
Nigeria, Uganda and Zambia as priority markets for entry, with a focus on building local market understanding for phased expansion into additional markets over time.Data consumption
Data consumption trends in India continue to remain robust, reflecting the deepening integration of digital services into everyday life. During the quarter ended March 2026, total wireless data traffic reached 78 EB, registering a healthy year-on-year increase of 31%, while average monthly data consumption per subscriber rose to 26.7 GB, growing by 20% over the previous year.The shift towards 5G networks has further accelerated this trend, with 5G data traffic nearly doubling during the period. In parallel, Fixed Wireless Access (FWA) is emerging as a meaningful growth driver, with 5G FWA users consuming substantially higher data compared to mobile-only subscribers. These trends underscore the rising requirement for enhanced network capacity, densification and high-quality telecom infrastructure across the country.Device adoption has accelerated significantly, with ~90% of smartphones shipped in 2025 being 5G-enabled and an estimated ~383 million active 5G-capable devices in the country, reflecting the rapid migration towards next-generation connectivity. 
Looking ahead, 5G subscriptions are 
expected to scale meaningfully, supported by government initiatives promoting enterprise and industry use cases. Industry estimates indicate that 5G subscriptions in India could reach nearly 980 million by 2030. These trends are expected to drive sustained investments in network expansion, densification and digital infrastructure.
5G rollout
5G rollout in India continues to gain momentum, with services now available across nearly 99.9% of districts and supported by widespread network expansion. Operators are increasingly focussing on network densification and capacity augmentation to support rising data traffic and evolving use cases.
5G subscribers as of March 2026

Network expansion
India offers a significant long-term network expansion opportunity, driven by rising connectivity requirements across both urban and rural markets. While urban teledensity at ~143% in the country remains relatively high, rural teledensity at ~60% highlights substantial headroom for network densification and coverage expansion across underserved geographies. The expansion of urban peripheries and increasing demand for seamless connectivity are reinforcing the need for reliable and scalable telecom infrastructure.Key Growth 
Drivers
In addition, there is headroom for operators 
to further expand their network given the difference in their footprints. The improving financial and operating position of a major customer, supported by recent policy measures and strengthening industry dynamics, is expected to accelerate network investments and rollout activity over the medium term. This is likely to drive incremental demand for towers, co-locations and related infrastructure services across the sector.01

Maintaining high network uptime and service 
reliability remains central to operations. We have further enhanced network resilience through proactive monitoring, predictive maintenance, and faster incident response, enabled by AI-led analytics, IoT integration, and real-time operational dashboards. These digital initiatives have improved network visibility, enabling quicker outage detection, more effective root-cause analysis, and efficient field execution.

Operational efficiency remains a core strategic priority, with a sustained focus on enhancing productivity, improving execution predictability and optimising overall cost structure. We achieve this through greater standardisation in design frameworks, governance, sharper execution and supply chain planning, and technology-led interventions.
Energy optimisation continues to be a key 
lever. Increased deployment of solar solutions, lithium-ion batteries and smart infrastructure solutions has helped improve uptime, reduce diesel dependency and lower operating costs. These initiatives, complemented by digital tools, automation, IoT-enabled monitoring, and value engineering, are driving sustainable efficiency gains and supporting long-term margin resilience.

 Industry-leading tenancy ratio1.62x
We benefit from strong economies of scale and operating leverage, resulting in one of the lowest unit operating costs in the industry. Incremental tenancies on existing towers drive significantly higher returns, as additional revenues are earned with marginal cost increases. With an industry-leading sharing ratio of 1.62x, Indus generates healthy returns and is positioned as a cost-efficient infrastructure partner, enabling us to offer a highly competitive value proposition to its customers.Pan-India presence with Pan-India presence with extensive reach
Indus Towers is among the largest telecom tower companies, with an extensive portfolio of towers and colocations and a presence across all telecom circles in India, enabling true pan-India coverage. This scale and network reach provide significant advantages to telecom operators by reducing time-to-market, lowering capital expenditure requirements, and optimising operating costs through shared infrastructure.

The performance for the year was complemented by 
strong sourcing capabilities and operational discipline, even amidst a dynamic global and domestic economic environment that continued to influence supply chains.
The global economic environment during the year 
remained measured, even as it navigated persistent geopolitical tensions, evolving trade dynamics and periodic volatility in energy markets. While inflationary pressures moderated compared to prior periods, uncertainty continued to shape global growth outlook.
Against this backdrop, India sustained strong growth 
momentum during FY26, with GDP expanding by ~7.7% (provisional estimates), supported by resilient consumption and continued capital investment. Inflation eased during the year and remained within the RBI’s target band, enabling a calibrated monetary policy approach to support growth while maintaining price stability. On the fiscal front, the Government maintained consolidation discipline, while continuing its strong emphasis on infrastructure development. Looking ahead, India is expected to maintain its strong growth trajectory, with RBI projecting GDP growth at ~6.6% in FY27, reinforcing its position as one of the fastest-growing major economies globally.
Digitialisation - a key theme
India’s infrastructure-led growth model remains 
a structural driver of its economic trajectory. Continued public investment, with capital expenditure at over `11 Tn in FY26 is driving expansion across roads, railways, logistics and urban infrastructure.
Urbanisation and formalisation trends are further 
reinforcing this transformation driving demand for seamless digital access.
Additionally, a key structural theme underpinning India’s 
growth is the rapid expansion of its digital economy. Digital adoption into everyday economic activity continues to deepen across payments, commerce, public services and enterprise operations, supported by strong policy initiatives and the scale of India’s digital public infrastructure. This digital shift is further complemented by the continued rapid rise in data consumption and rollout of 5G networks, enabling faster, more reliable and high-speed connectivity.
Regulatory landscape
The sustained surge in data usage is driving the need 
for greater network capacity and wider coverage across mobile networks, making the rapid rollout of passive infrastructure a critical enabler. Encouragingly, Government policy remains supportive of this expansion, with a series of structural reforms aimed at improving ease of deployment while balancing long-term sustainability considerations.
A key development was the introduction of a proposed 
incentive framework, aimed at encouraging wider adoption of the updated Right of Way (RoW) Rules, 2024. This is enabling streamlining of approval processes, enhancing implementation consistency across geographies, and reducing deployment timelines.
In parallel, the ongoing implementation of the Green 
Energy Open Access policy is expected to play a critical role in structurally lowering energy costs and improving sustainability outcomes for infrastructure providers. Developments in the power ecosystem are also moving towards greater digitisation and transparency, with accelerated rollout of smart metering infrastructure expected to enhance energy visibility and enable more efficient cost management over time.
At a broader level, Government-led 
initiatives in areas such as artificial intelligence, quantum technologies and innovation are accelerating the adoption of next-generation capabilities. Together, these developments are reinforcing the role of telecom networks as foundational infrastructure supporting India’s transition towards a digital economy.
The year also saw the Government’s 
intervention on AGR dues relating to Vodafone Idea. The revised framework is expected to provide meaningful financial relief to the operator and support a sustainable industry structure. This, in turn, enables a renewed focus on network investments, with the operator outlining plans to strengthen coverage and accelerate technology upgrades.
In this evolving landscape, Indus 
Towers remains well positioned to support the deployment of digital infrastructure for the next phase of India’s growth. Our scale, strong execution capabilities and deep customer partnerships enable us to efficiently deliver infrastructure solutions. We are also strengthening our focus on automation, data-led decision-making and advanced digital technologies to enhance operational efficiency. Together, these capabilities allow us to deliver efficient, resilient and future-ready infrastructure, supporting our customers’ network ambitions and the broader evolution of the telecom ecosystem.
Robust performance, continued value 
creation
FY26 was another strong year for 
Indus Towers with the inherent strength of the core business coming to the fore. Our ability to offer a unique value proposition to our customers continued to help us remain their preferred partner, as evidenced by our substantial market share in their rollouts.
Our continued tower additions and 
meaningful co-location additions took our overall base to 264,514 macro towers and 428,014 co-locations respectively. This translated into a healthy financial performance across all parameters.
Total revenues were at `325 billion, 
growing 7.9% Y-o-Y, while core revenues increased 9.0% Y-o-Y to `209 billion. The acquisition of towers from Bharti Airtel in the preceding year also aided the growth momentum. Reported EBITDA decreased by 13.8% to `180 billion, and Reported Profit after Tax declined 28.1% to `71.5 billion. The underlying performance remained strong as headline financials for FY25 were influenced by clearance of overdues amounting to roughly `51 billion by a major customer. Adjusted for this, EBITDA and Profit after Tax were up 11.4% and 13.0%, respectively.
Your Company generated free cash 
flow of over `37 billion during the year, reflecting the strength of its operating model, disciplined capital allocation and sustained focus on financial prudence. In line with our commitment to delivering long-term value to shareholders, the Board has recommended a final dividend of `14 per share.
International Expansion
During the year, we announced 
foray into select markets of Africa, marking an important milestone in our long-term growth strategy. These markets offer strong growth potential, supported by rising data demand and evolving telecom infrastructure requirements. Our proven execution capabilities, experience in building cost-efficient passive infrastructure, and the deep presence of an anchor customer provide us with a distinct competitive advantage as we scale our operations.
Social commitment a key focus area
Beyond our core business operations, 
we remain deeply committed to driving meaningful social impact. Under our flagship programme, Saksham, implemented in partnership with the Bharti Airtel Foundation, we supported over 30 Satya Bharti schools and 1,100 Government schools across multiple states and union territories through the Quality Support Programme.
Through our other flagship 
programme, Pragati, we undertook

Looking ahead

MESSAGE FROM MD AND CEO
The Government’s continued support for maintaining a 
three-private-player market structure, including the grant of significant relief on AGR dues to a major operator, has improved the long-term outlook of the sector.
Your Company witnessed healthy demand for new 
towers and co-location additions, translating into robust operational performance during the year. The growth was supported by continued network expansion and 5G densification as data consumption growth was recorded at 25%. Our ability to deliver at scale, combined with a sharp focus on operational excellence and customer-centricity enabled us to further strengthen our position as a preferred infrastructure partner in the telecom ecosystem.
Secular Growth Environment
Demand for data continues to remain strong with 
ongoing migration from 2G to 4G and 5G, growing 5G smartphone shipments and underlying increase in usage for smartphone customers. The average monthly data consumption per user for the quarter ended March 2026 touched ~26.7 GB, growing 20% YoY. In the same period, growth in the total data consumption was 31%.
Total 5G customer base stood at 427 million as of 
March 2026, with an addition of 182 million seen over the previous year. To support this rising adoption, telecom operators rolled out ~56,000 5G base stations during the year compared to ~40,000 during FY25, bringing the total count to ~531,000. The sustained deployment of 5G equipment is a key contributor to our overall loading revenues.
Robust Operating Performance
Your Company reported strong operating performance in 
FY26. Net additions during the year stood at 15,209 macro towers and 22,579 co-locations, expanding our portfolio to 264,514 towers and 428,014 co-locations, while maintaining an industry-leading sharing factor of 1.62x.
The robust operating performance also resulted in 
a healthy free cash generation during the year. I am pleased to share that the board approved resumption of dividends with a payout of nearly 100% of FY26 free cash flow, backed by confidence on Company’s sustained cashflow generation and improving visibility on potential growth prospects.
Steady Progress across Strategic Priorities
Market Share Expansion
In FY26, we further strengthened our market position, 
reinforcing our status as a preferred partner for major customers. A key growth driver was the pick-up in rollouts by a major customer following its fund raise in preceding year. We also capitalised on opportunities for relocating a major customer’s sites to our portfolio, further enhancing our market presence.
Our performance was underpinned by a consistent 
focus on reliability, competitive pricing, and execution excellence. Stringent quality standards, targeted technical interventions, and customised solutions helped strengthen delivery outcomes.
We continued to build momentum in other business 
segments. We improved our ranking during the year to achieve leadership position in the In-building Solution (IBS) space through a proactive acquisition strategy, while our Distributed Antenna System (DAS) business saw increased deployments across metros, tunnels, and highways. With a strong focus on build-to-suit solutions and technological advancement, we remain confident on long term growth prospects.Cost Efficiency
Our efforts are channelised to drive 
operational excellence by delivering structural improvements across both operating and capital expenditure. During the year, we accelerated the adoption of digital tools, standardised processes and strengthened governance frameworks, improved planning accuracy and streamlined execution. Field productivity remained a key focus area, with digital enablement, optimised site allocation and greater centralisation helping reduce redundancies and improve workforce productivity.
We scaled deployment of 
energy-efficient solutions, including solar integration across ~42,400 sites, and accelerated adoption of lithium-ion batteries, lowering total cost of ownership. These initiatives are structurally reducing diesel dependency, improving uptime and moderating our energy cost profile.
On the capex front, we maintained 
a disciplined investment approach through stronger execution controls and value engineering-led design optimisation.
Collectively, these measures are 
enhancing cost predictability, improving operational efficiency and positioning us well for sustained margin resilience.
Network Uptime
Ensuring network uptime is key to 
enhancing customer satisfaction and quality of service. With our advanced digital infrastructure powered by AI and analytics, we maintained high uptime at an industry-leading 99.97% in FY2025-26. This was achieved despite several catastrophic and weather-related challenges, which highlights dedication and perseverance of our teams on the ground. I would also like to recognise the dedication and resilience of our field teams, who have delivered remarkably under challenging conditions.
Digital Transformation
Our digital transformation agenda 
is reshaping how we operate. Through the deployment of AI, automation, advanced analytics, digital twins and IoT-enabled solutions, we are creating a more intelligent, efficient and responsive network. These capabilities are improving uptime, strengthening field execution, enabling real-time asset visibility and driving faster, data-led decisions. As a result, we are enhancing operational performance, elevating customer experience and reinforcing our market leadership.
Embedding Sustainability
Sustainability remains integral 
to strategic decision making. We have established a structured decarbonisation pathway aligned to our net-zero ambition for 2050.
We continued to make progress on 
our people agenda, strengthening diversity and capabilities across the organisation. Gender diversity improved to 18.3% in FY2025-26 from 16.2% in FY2024-25, supported by focussed inclusion initiatives and a strong emphasis on enhancing diversity at leadership levels. Safety of our workforce is paramount to us. We rolled out targeted campaigns and specialised training, with a focus on road safety and safe practices for technicians working at heights.
Our partnership with Bharti 
Airtel Foundation remains central to our social impact agenda, driving transformative initiatives in education and digital inclusion that are empowering children and communities with greater access to learning opportunities and a brighter future.
On governance, we further 
strengthened our framework through improved disclosures, reinforcing accountability to all stakeholders. We uphold our code of conduct across employees and partners, with zero tolerance for non-compliance.
Africa Expansion
During the year, we marked a 
significant milestone in our journey with entry into Africa, aligned with our strategy to diversify revenue and participate in markets with strong growth potential for digital infrastructure. This decision comes at a critical point to leverage our robust financial position and deep-rooted presence of our anchor customer across the markets. Moreover, we strongly believe, this will further expand infra sharing model in Africa, the way Indus Towers enabled it in India many years ago by building efficient network infra for telcos.

your Company, underpinned by the robustness of our business model and our ability to consistently deliver value in a dynamic operating environment. The year was marked by execution excellence and sustained momentum in network deployments across our key customers.Sustaining

Looking forward
The outlook for India’s telecom and 
digital infrastructure sector remains compelling, underpinned by the confluence of growing connectivity needs even in deepest corner of the country, democratisation of data and rapid 5G adoption. India continues to be among the most data-intensive markets globally, with tariffs at approximately USD 0.16 per GB supporting sustained high consumption.
5G subscriptions are projected to reach 
~980 million by 2030 and comprise a dominant share of the overall subscriber base, as per the Ericsson Mobility Report. This, in turn, is driving the need for robust and scalable telecom infrastructure, reinforcing a strong and sustained demand outlook for the sector.
We are excited about our entry into 
Africa, which represents a new avenue of growth for the Company.
As we look ahead, we remain confident 
in our ability to build on this momentum, supported by our focus on operational excellence, disciplined capital allocation and technology-led transformation. We remain committed to enabling our customers’ evolving network needs while delivering sustainable long-term value for all stakeholders.

We view materiality assessment as a discipline that strengthens long-term value creation. Our process 
helps us understand issues that have a direct impact on our performance, influence stakeholder expectations and guide responsible decision-making. We began our structured materiality journey in FY22 in alignment with the Global Reporting Initiative standards, and we continue to refine this approach through regular stakeholder consultations held every three years. In FY25, we advanced this framework through a double materiality assessment, evaluating each topic through two lenses – its impact on our business and its wider impact on society and the environment. This approach enables us to prioritise ESG issues with greater clarity and ensures that our strategy reflects both organisational priorities and broader sustainability outcomes. During FY26, we developed action plans across our key material issues, translating materiality insights into targeted initiatives, measurable outcomes, and strategic ESG interventions.
References to the targeted actions, initiatives, and outcomes arising from this assessment are integrated 
across the respective capitals throughout this report.
Addressing the priorities 
of a transforming futureDOUBLE MATERIALITY ASSESSMENT Translating material insights into action
Double materiality enables us to assess sustainability topics through the combined 
lens of stakeholder impact and financial relevance. The assessment strengthens clarity on issues that matter most to our business and ecosystem, including climate action, safety, cybersecurity, human capital, technology, innovation and energy management. These insights guide sharper governance oversight, risk responses and long-term value creation priorities.
Impact materiality
A sustainability issue is considered material from an impact standpoint 
if it has, or may have, meaningful effects on people or the environment across the short, medium and long term. This includes impacts directly caused or contributed to by the organisation, as well as those linked to activities across the value chain, spanning upstream and downstream services, operations, and business relationships.
Key outcomes of the assessment
The findings of the double materiality assessment were presented to the Board ESG Committee, providing clear visibility into emerging shifts across our risk and impact landscape. Cybersecurity saw the most significant movement, rising from a low-priority to a high-priority material issue. This elevation reflects the increasing complexity of digital threats and growing expectations around data privacy, continuity planning, and cyber resilience.
Other critical issues, such as climate change, GHG emissions, health 
and safety, innovation, and human rights, remain high-priority and continue to shape our strategic focus. These topics are monitored closely to ensure alignment with evolving regulatory requirements and stakeholder priorities.
We maintain a robust mitigation framework to address these material 
risks and opportunities, and we are strengthening it further in response to the heightened risk profile of cybersecurity. Enhanced controls, governance mechanisms, and monitoring systems are being implemented to ensure a more resilient and future-ready posture.Financial materiality
A sustainability issue is financially material when it poses risks or opportunities that may influence future financial performance, position, or cash flows over different time horizons. The assessment focusses on information that is relevant to primary users of financial reports as they evaluate the organisation’s ability to generate long-term value and allocate resources effectively.01

Approach to double materiality
To perform double materiality assessment, following steps are taken:

 �Financial indices, rankingWe complemented our desktop research with insights from the topics identified in our previous materiality exercise. To fully integrate the financial and risk viewpoint, we also incorporated the outcomes of the risk register into the assessment. The resulting list of 22 topics reflects areas that can influence the environment, society, or the economy, while also presenting risks and opportunities for the business. Each topic includes clear definitions and subtopics to ensure comprehensive coverage of Indus’s activities and operations throughout the assessment.Identify the Issues most Material01
We engaged with both internal and external stakeholders to gather qualitative information.We prioritised stakeholder groups based on their influence on Indus and the extent to which our activities affect them. Online surveys for both impact and financial materiality were shared with all stakeholder categories. We then conducted in-depth qualitative interviews with selected internal and external stakeholders to validate the survey findings and gather deeper insights for the subsequent risk and opportunity assessment.
Prior to each interview, stakeholders received a long 
list of potentially material topics and were asked to identify the most significant impacts, risks, and opportunities. The interviews explored their views on our sustainability priorities and expectations around the way we communicate our performance and commitments.Stakeholder engagement

ESG Governance Framework
A robust, multi-tiered ESG governance framework embeds sustainability as a core organisational priority, and 
ensures ESG functions as a strategic enabler, not merely as a compliance obligation. It integrates oversight at the Board and management levels and governance at the operational-level through cross-functional ESG councils and circle-level interventions. This structure enables effective on-ground execution, creates accountability, encourages collaboration and empowers teams across all levels.

Related party transactions are

Regular disclosures and adherence to global best practices strengthen governance and mitigate potential conflicts of interest.Managing conflicts of interest is essential to maintaining integrity and objectivity in decision-making. Data privacyWe maintain a comprehensive cybersecurity strategy 
aligned with international standards to protect our infrastructure, digital assets, and user environments. The framework includes a formal Information Security Policy, third-party security risk assessments (TPSRM), and regular training to strengthen internal cyber awareness. Employees are engaged through initiatives such as Information Security Awareness Week, Cybersecurity Awareness Month, cyber games, mascot-based campaigns, and The Circle Infosec League, building vigilance and reducing risks linked to human error.Our security investments continue to scale with evolving threats. Protections such as DDoS mitigation, Web Application Firewall (WAF), and Network Access Control (NAC) safeguard network entry points and restrict access to authorised users and devices. End-user systems are secured through Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR), Data Leakage Prevention (DLP), Secure Web Gateway (SWG), Mobile Device Management (MDM), encryption, and Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA). These layered controls support proactive threat detection, maintain operational continuity, and protect data integrity across our digital landscape.
We view data privacy as a core responsibility that uphold stakeholder trust. 
All personal and digital data belonging to customers, employees, and partners is managed in line with applicable laws and our organisational values.
Our Information Security Policy, available to all employees, sets clear protocols 
to protect the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of information. The implementation of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDPA), along with our Data Privacy Policy further strengthens our compliance framework by reinforcing safeguards related to data access, storage, and sharing. Indus Towers follows a robust Enterprise Risk 
Management framework to proactively identify and address emerging and evolving risks across economic, environmental, social, governance, cyber security and market domains. Our approach strengthens risk resilience, supports strategic decision-making and enables long-term value creation. Guided by innovation, technology and collaboration, we aim to convert risks into opportunities that support sustainable growth and contribute to India’s digital transformation.
Strengthening resilience 
for a connected futureRISK MANAGEMENT 
Risk Management Framework
Given the scale of our operations and 
the critical infrastructure we manage, proactive risk identification and mitigation remain key priorities. Our approach combines top-down oversight with bottom-up inputs. The risk management framework is structured to systematically identify, assess, address and report key risks across critical business dimensions. It supports sound corporate governance, strengthens management accountability and promotes transparency.Process step What we do Outcome
Defined risk scope 
and assessment basisAlign risk identification with business strategy, operating priorities, regulatory environment and stakeholder expectations
ESTABLISH CONTEXT
Updated risk registerIdentify risks across functions, sites, assets, customers, technology, people, compliance, cyber security, ESG and market developments
IDENTIFY RISKS
Prioritised key riskEvaluate likelihood, impact, severity and business relevance
ASSESS RISKS
Clear mitigation roadmapDefine controls, action plans, owners, resources and timelines
PRIORITISE RESPONSE
Risk status reporting to management and Board-level committeesTrack progress through reviews, dashboards, audits, KPIs and mitigation scores
TREAT AND MANAGE RISKS
Stronger controls and resilient operationsIncorporate learnings from incidents, audits, market shifts and emerging risks
MONITOR, REPORT AND IMPROVE

Connected, AI-powered Network Operations
At the core of this transformation is iDoT, which 
has evolved into a critical digital backbone for Indus Towers’ operations. Its scale-up, supported by widespread IoT-enabled connectivity, has enabled real-time visibility into asset performance, energy consumption, and site conditions.This connectivity allows towers to stream live data – from fuel sensors, smart meters, backhaul systems, and power equipment – into the Tower Operations Centre, supporting preventive maintenance and faster corrective actions.Building on this, the deployment of AI and machine-learning models has strengthened operations through proactive outage identification, automated root-cause analysis, and improved resolution effectiveness. Initiatives such as AI-enabled voice agents and computer vision–based validation have further enhanced field productivity, standardisation, and compliance.
Together, these capabilities are enabling a 
shift from periodic monitoring to continuous, data-driven operations – progressing from reactive to preventive management, with increasing adoption of predictive capabilities.
Additionally, we are standardising ways 
of working across circles by consolidating specialised capability at a central level through dedicated Centres of Excellence (CoEs). This is creating uniform standards and better coordination across the network.
Our Tower Engineering Centre (TEC) CoE has 
been instrumental in optimising tower loading decision-making. A centralised hub housing comprehensive structural and design data of our entire tower portfolio, advanced software and expert engineers at TEC streamline tower loading assessments, enabling swift pre-clearance and faster response to customer co-location requests.
Connecting India’s frontier 
Expanded network reach with deployments in remote, high-altitude border regions, including Nubra Valley, Punguk-Hanle village along the Indo-China border, and Kharu Tehsil in Ladakh with elevations of up to ~14,600 ft. above sea level

In-building solutions and small cells
In-building solutions (IBS), including Distributed Antenna Systems (DAS) and small 
cells, are increasingly critical to addressing indoor coverage requirements across India’s rapidly evolving urban landscape – spanning commercial complexes, transit hubs, and high-density public infrastructure.
Enhanced execution capability enabled faster roll-outs, increased deployment 
momentum, and strengthened positioning in the segment. We remain focussed on scaling this segment in line with evolving network requirements.
 Expansion into new infrastructure formats – Special projects 
We are deploying innovative, location-specific solutions to improve connectivity across complex and high-density environments like metro tunnels, congested markets, elevated roads and flyovers, NHAI tunnels, airports and buildings. With solutions like leaky feeder, MU-RU, outdoor/pole-mounted/hybrid DAS and overhead equipment, we are addressing unique coverage challenges.
In FY26, the business gathered momentum with increased deployments in metros, 
tunnels and highways. Our focus on delivering build-to-suit solutions and advancing technology positions this segment for further growth.
 Institutional Acquisition
Institutional sites are critical to widening our network coverage. Our dedicated Enterprise Vertical offers bundled telecom and adjacent infrastructure solutions to central and state governments, military establishments, educational institutions, and municipalities to pursue institutional site acquisition.
Earth Stations: A Satcom infrastructure Play
Built a strong presence in India’s rapidly growing satellite broadband sector by delivering customised ground and rooftop Earth Station infrastructure for leading global Satcom operators, including OneWeb, Amazon, and Starlink. Backed by end-to-end capabilities spanning commercial engagement, engineering, regulatory approvals, readiness assessments, and project execution, the business has emerged as a trusted infrastructure partner. The pipeline remains strong, with two Amazon LEO Earth Stations nearing completion, one Starlink Earth Station under construction, and 3–4 additional projects in various stages of development.
FTTH and Fibre Infrastructure: Scaling Last-Mile Connectivity
Expanded its presence in India’s last-mile digital connectivity segment through FTTH, FTTB, overhead fibre (OHF), and telecom pole infrastructure solutions. In FY26, secured engagements deploying over 10,000 FTTH poles and ~100 km of OHF across five states. With integrated capabilities in pole supply, installation, and RoW facilitation, the business enables faster, cost-efficient aerial fibre rollouts and supports broadband expansion across key markets.

embedding AI and machine learning capabilities to convert operational data into predictive and prescriptive insights. Instead of relying only on manual reviews or reactive interventions, teams are increasingly supported by analytics that prioritise risks, identify exceptions and guide targeted action. The result is sharper decision-making, better allocation of field resources and faster resolution of operational issues.

Next-generation site intelligenceDigitising the landlord lifecycle
Drone-based site intelligenceOur digital transformation is extending into advanced site intelligence through Site Service Image and 
drone-based surveying. Together, these capabilities improve the precision of planning, engineering assessment, capital deployment and field safety by creating richer, more reliable views of site-level conditions. 
During the year, we also completed a proof of concept for drone-based site surveying across more than 350 
sites, capturing over 183 parameters per site. High-resolution, as-built 3D digital twins were generated, with automated detection of structural defects, RF blockages and tower-loading validation.
Drone-based intelligence reduces reliance on manual inspection, improves planning accuracy and enhances 
field safety. The depth of site-level data generated also creates a strong foundation for future AI-led planning, optimisation and asset lifecycle management.Site Service Image - Digital Twin
Site Service Image has been operationalised as a unified platform for site intelligence. It integrates data from multiple enterprise systems, including iDOT, iSQ, Enterprise Asset Management, Oracle Billing and Revenue Management and iMAP, consolidating site operations, asset information, loading parameters, financial metrics and activity records into a single trusted view.

iAssist

It also strengthens consistency in task communication, tracking and closure, enabling better coordination between central operations and field teams.

Climate Action 
Climate Strategy
Our climate strategy is guided by an ambitious 
decarbonisation plan with medium and long-term targets aligned to our Net Zero 2050 goal’, validated by the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi). The roadmap positions us among the early adopters of science-based climate action in the telecom infrastructure sector.
Further, our ‘Zero Goal Hai’ campaign affirms our 
commitment to zero emissions, waste, harm, and bias. We strengthen accountability, regulatory compliance and long-term climate resilience through policies on environmental protection and sustainable sourcing, performance linked remuneration and Board-approved ESG governance.
Climate considerations are integrated into business 
planning, infrastructure investments and operational decision-making to strengthen long-term resilience and value creation.Climate change is identified as a material business risk with implications for infrastructure resilience, energy 
security, and long-term value creation. We systematically identify, assess, and manage climate-related risks through adaptation and mitigation measures embedded in our sustainability strategy.
Climate Change Adaptation and Mitigation
Climate Governance 
Climate-related risks and opportunities are governed through a Board-led governance structure, supported by the Management.  The Board and its ESG Committee provide strategic oversight, while the MD&CEO integrates ESG into business strategy. The Audit and Risk Committee reviews risk regularly. 
At the Management level, ESG initiatives are 
implemented across the operations, with monthly KPI  monitoring ensuring effective execution and continuous improvement. 
Performance-linked accountability mechanisms further 
support effective delivery of climate-related priorities across the organisation.

Scenario Analysis
We conducted IFRS-S2 aligned scenario analysis to assess climate-related physical and transition risks as well 
as the associated opportunities across various time horizons. The assessment evaluated plausible impacts of those risks on our infrastructure, operations and business continuity, helping us develop informed adaptation and mitigation measures.

Risk Review
Physical and Transition Risk Mitigation
Physical risks such as floods, cyclones and extreme 
weather events. are mitigated through adaptive measures and controls right at the inception of the project. A Business Continuity plan (BCP) ensures preparedness, response, and recovery from potential disruptions. Risk Management
Climate change-related risks are identified, assessed and prioritised, and managed using a ERM-integrated company-wide risk management framework that covers strategic (Climate and ESG-related risks), operational, compliance, and financial risks. Each risk is evaluated and prioritised based on its likelihood and impact to define mitigation actions, which are monitored continuously and reviewed quarterly by Risk Management Steering Committee (RMSC) and Board Risk Management Committee. Insights from climate risk assessment and scenario analysis are incorporated into Enterprise Risk Management, business strategy, infrastructure resilience planning and capital allocation, supporting informed adaptation and long-term business resilience.

Waste Reduction Initiatives at Offices
Teams across all our offices implement sustainable waste management practices. Waste is segregated, 
managed and safely disposed of in compliance with environmental regulations issued by the state and local municipal authorities.
Plastic Waste 
� Eliminated single-use plastics in routine operations 
� Replaced plastic water bottles with glass and stainless-steel  alternatives
� Conduct regular audits to monitor and reduce plastic use
Paper Waste 
� Adopted paperless claims and print-free event management to reduce printing and associated emissions
� Introduced hand dryers to reduce paper towel consumption
� Drove employee awareness on sustainable practices at work and in daily lifeCircular Resource Recovery
We have partnered with a specialised 
sanitary recycling facility to ensure environmentally responsible recovery of sanitary waste through an efficient, smokeless recycling process. Recovered plastic is repurposed into utility products, while residual waste is converted into recyclable paper and stationery, reducing emissions compared to landfilling and incineration. 
Food Waste
We track food waste daily to reduce its 
generation and encourage responsible consumption. Employee awareness is driven through sensitisation messages showing daily waste levels and their potential to feed many people.
Responsible Site Decommissioning and 
Material Repurposing
We promote circularity by redeploying 
dismantled towers and refurbishing components for secondary operational use, extending asset life and reducing resource consumption. Materials that cannot be reused or refurbished, are sent for recycling, while disposal through authorised recyclers in considered only as a last resort.

Biodiversity is not currently identified as a material topic for Indus Towers; however, we 
recognise its increasing relevance to long-term business and environmental resilience. Operating across diverse geographies, we seek to minimise ecological disruption and embed environmental considerations into project planning and execution from the outset.
Protecting Natural EcosystemsOur biodiversity approach follows a structured mitigation hierarchy: Avoid, Minimise, Restore, and Offset, helping us minimise ecological impacts and support ecosystem preservation and restoration. Biodiversity and Land Use
We proactively identify sites located within or near protected zones and strictly comply with environmental regulations to conserve natural habitats and restore ecosystems. A quarterly biodiversity tracking mechanism enables continuous monitoring, risk identification and corrective actions where required, aligning our commitment to net zero deforestation. We undertake plantation of three trees for every unavoidable tree removed to help mitigate environmental impacts. We have pledged to plant and nurture 1 million trees by 2027. 7.5 Lakh saplings were planted through our CSR programme till FY26.Avoid Minimise Restore OffsetOur Biodiversity Approach

The evolving telecom sector demands learning that is continuous, contextual and connected directly to the

Learning Framework
We place strong emphasis on continuous learning, enabling employees across all levels to enhance their technical, behavioural and leadership capabilities. Training needs identification (TNI) anchors our learning and development strategy, enabling targeted capability building aligned with evolving business priorities and future skill requirements.
Delivered through a blend of self-paced digital courses, classroom sessions and expert-led virtual 
programmes, our learning interventions saw strong participation across all levels.
Driving Impact through Integrated Learning 
and Talent Frameworks
Training Needs Identification (TNI) serves as 
the cornerstone of our learning and development strategy, enabling targeted capability building aligned with evolving business priorities and future skill requirements. We have institutionalised a structured framework that integrates 16 identified future skills across key focus areas, including team and role-based development, succession planning, and the acceleration of high-potential talent – ensuring a strong, future-ready leadership and talent pipeline.
Our integrated performance and talent

Health and Safety:  
Zero Compromise Across All Sites
Safety for us is not just a compliance function, it is a moral commitment. Our Environment, Safety & Health 
(ESH) framework, grounded in the principles of Zero Fatality, Zero Fire and Zero Collapse and supported by the leadership commitment, governs every operational decision.
Health and Safety Management System
Health and Safety Management System
Our health and safety framework integrates prevention, governance, technology and continuous improvement to protect our people and operations.The Company has implemented a comprehensive Occupational Health and Safety Management System covering all employees, field staff, contract workers, riggers and partners. It applies across sites, towers, warehouses, construction activities and field travel. Systematic identification, reporting, and timely closure of workplace hazards are carried out to maintain a safe and compliant working environment.
Hazard Identification & Risk 
Assessment
Proactive hazard identification 
through HIRA, and scheduled preventive maintenance enable risks to be identified and mitigated in a prompt manner.
Safety Controls
Risks are eliminated or minimised 
through a structured application of the hierarchy of controls.
Hazard Reporting and Incident 
Management
Digital reporting systems, root cause 
investigations, corrective actions and SOP improvements enable timely hazard resolution and strengthen incident prevention.
Reinforcing Safety Culture
Mandatory ESH onboarding and 
regular training, toolbox talks, competency development and recognition programmes embed a strong safety culture.Mandatory Permit to Work and Restricted Access
High risk activities are governed by a 
robust Permit-to-Work system (PTW), with access restricted to trained, certified and authorised personnel under competent supervision.
ESH Index Monitoring and 
Continuous Improvement
Continuous monitoring of leading 
and lagging indicators, coupled with incident learnings, drives ongoing improvements in ESH performance.
EHS Audits and Compliance
Regular audits, governance reviews 
and strict compliance measures reinforce operational safety, emergency preparedness and partner accountability.
Safety Digitisation
AI-enabled PTW, digital platforms and 
real-time dashboards enhance safety governance, compliance monitoring, reporting and decision-making.

Policy Partnership and 
Industry Leadership
Government institutions and regulatory bodies play a critical role in enabling India’s digital transformation. 
At Indus Towers, we view this relationship as a strategic partnership that helps strengthen connectivity, support policy development and create long-term value for society. 
We engage regularly with district, state, and central 
authorities through consultations, industry forums, seminars, formal representations, and periodic meetings. Our active participation in DLTC and State Broadband Committee meetings helps address critical issues related to policy implementation, energy access, operational restrictions, and coercive actions. These engagements enable us to represent industry perspectives, anticipate regulatory developments, and support a conducive policy environment for India’s digital infrastructure.
At the state level, sustained advocacy has facilitated 
resolution of issues relating to property taxes, tower sealing and demolition, municipal permissions, local levies, and electricity connectivity. These efforts also led to several favourable circulars and administrative directives, creating a more enabling environment for network expansion.Through sustained collaboration with policymakers and industry bodies such as DIPA, COAI, BIF, and ASSOCHAM, nearly 90% of Right of Way (RoW) challenges across India have been addressed, significantly improving telecom infrastructure deployment. The implementation of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and RoW Rules, 2024 established a unified national framework that streamlined approvals, enabled digital processes, reduced compliance costs, and strengthened protection of telecom infrastructure.
During FY26, the Company actively engaged 
with DoT, LSAs, MoP, CEA, SERCs, and State Governments to drive reforms that support infrastructure growth, improve ease of doing business, and accelerate digital connectivity. Its advocacy contributed to effective implementation

2. a.  Does the entity ha ve procedures in place for sustainable sourcing? (Yes/No)
 
  Indus has a w
ell‑defined “Sustainable Procurement Policy” and established procedures for sustainable 
sourcing across its value chain. A structured framework is in place to ensure that environmental, 
social, and ethical considerations are systematically integrated into sourcing and partner management practices.
 
  Sus
tainable sourcing procedures begin at the partner onboarding stage, where suppliers and 
service partners are evaluated through comprehensive due‑diligence and assessment processes. Depending on the nature of engagement, these assessments cover business conduct, statutory and regulatory compliance, environmental management, safety and health practices (‘ESH’), and ethical standards. For supply and infrastructure partners, evaluations go beyond conventional checks and include audits of facilities, operational processes, safety systems, environmental practices, and compliance mechanisms.
 
  P
ost onboarding, partners are subject to ongoing monitoring, audits, and governance oversight to 
ensure continued adherence to responsible sourcing policies. Performance assessments and rating programs periodically review parameters such as safe working practices, use of personal protective equipment (‘PPE’), contractual compliance, and risk management measures. These reviews help identify gaps and enable targeted improvement actions.
 
  T
o strengthen accountability, the entity has implemented preventive controls, including annual 
gating criteria and mandatory self‑certification against the Code of Conduct. These mechanisms ensure business continuity only with partners who meet defined environmental, social, and ethical 
Principle 2Businesses should provide goods and services in a manner that is 
sustainable and safe.

10. Health and saf ety management system 
a.
  W
hether an occupational health and safety management system has been implemented by the entity? 
(Yes/ No). If yes, what is the coverage of such a system?
 
 Y
es, the Company has implemented a comprehensive Occupational Health and Safety (‘OHS’) Management 
System. The system is designed to ensure a safe and healthy working environment across all operations 
and activities.
 
 T
he coverage of the OHS Management System is extensive and includes all employees, field staff, contract 
workers, riggers, and business partners. It is applicable across all operational areas, including sites, telecom towers, warehouses, construction activities, and field travel.
 
 T
he system is governed through a structured ESH framework, which is supported by:
 yA formal ESH Policy demonstrating strong leadership commitment towards achieving Zero Fatality, Zero Fire, and Zero Collapse; and
 yClearly defined Life Saving Rules (‘LSR’) applicable to all high ‑risk activities.
 In addition, the C
ompany actively promotes a culture of safety through:
 yNational safety campaigns;
 yLeadership ‑led safety broadcasting calls; and
 yRegular sharing of incident learnings to drive continuous improvement.
 
  T
his integrated approach ensures consistent safety standards, risk mitigation, and continuous 
reinforcement of safe practices across the organisation.

routine basis by the entity?
 
 T
he Company follows structured and proactive processes to identify work ‑
related hazards and assess risks

 P

This includes activities such as electrical work, work at height, material handling, excavation, etc.
 
 Hier

 Oper

continuous improvement in occupational health and safety performance.

 Describe the int
ernal mechanisms in place to redress grievances related to human rights issues.
 
 Indus is c
ommitted to providing a safe, inclusive, and respectful workplace, with zero tolerance for any 
form of human rights violations. To uphold this commitment, the Company has established robust internal mechanisms to effectively address and redress grievances related to human rights issues.
 
 T
he Company promotes an open
‑
door policy, encouraging employees and stakeholders to freely raise 
concerns without fear of retaliation. A well
‑
defined grievance redressal framework is in place, enabling 
employees, retainers/consultants, associates, suppliers and business partners to report any concerns or violations. Such concerns can be escalated through the Ombudsperson mechanism, ensuring an independent and impartial review process.
 
 In addition, the C
ompany has implemented a comprehensive POSH Policy. Any complaints under this 
Policy can be reported to the Chairperson of the ICC who is responsible for handling such matters in accordance with applicable laws and internal guidelines.
 
 All r
eported cases are addressed with utmost seriousness and are governed by the principles of natural 
justice, confidentiality, sensitivity, non
‑
retaliation and fairness. The Company ensures that concerns are 
managed with empathy and diligence, while also striving for timely resolution and closure. Further details on grievance mechanisms are outlined in the Company’s Whistle Blower Policy which is accessible on the Company’s website as well POSH Policy available on Company’s intranet.
 
 During the r
eporting year, the Company also conducted training sessions on human rights to enhance 
awareness among internal stakeholders regarding their rights, responsibilities and available grievance redressal mechanisms.

  Briefly describe the w
aste management practices adopted in your establishments. Describe the strategy 
adopted by your company to reduce usage of hazardous and toxic chemicals in your products and 
processes and the practices adopted to manage such wastes.
 
 T
he Company undertakes periodic assessments of its assets through independent chartered engineering 
firms to evaluate their residual life. Based on these assessments, targeted interventions are carried out to refurbish and revive assets, thereby extending their useful lifespan and promoting resource efficiency. Assets identified as end
‑
of
‑
life are disposed of in an environmentally responsible manner through Pollution 
Control Board (PCB)–authorised recyclers, facilitated via a Government of India enterprise (MSTC).
 
 T
he Company follows a structured waste management framework anchored in the principles of reduce, 
reuse, and recycle (3R). Hazardous waste at Indus primarily include used lubricating oil, battery waste, and other regulated materials. A defined mechanism is in place for the safe handling, storage, transportation, and disposal of such wastes in compliance with applicable regulations, ensuring minimal environmental impact.
 
 In addition t
o hazardous waste management, robust systems have been established for the segregation, 
monitoring, and reporting of administrative waste streams such as plastic and food waste. These practices promote responsible waste handling, enable improved resource recovery, and contribute to enhancing overall sustainability performance.
 
 T
o further minimise the use of hazardous and toxic substances, the Company focusses on optimising 
operational processes, promoting the use of safer alternatives where feasible, and strengthening lifecycle
‑
based asset and material management practices.

‑
specific continuity strategies. These are

1. Describe the mechanisms in plac e to receive and respond to consumer complaints and feedback 
 
 W
ith a clear objective of delivering best
‑
in
‑
class services, the organisation places strong emphasis on 
understanding Customer needs, addressing their concerns promptly, and providing effective resolutions. A well
‑
defined and multi
‑
layered governance framework is in place to ensure structured engagement with 
Customers and timely handling of complaints and feedback.
 
 T
he organisation maintains continuous engagement with Customers through daily, weekly, and monthly 
interactions at both Head Office and Circle levels. These structured interactions enable proactive identification of issues, real
‑
time query resolution, and ongoing service improvement. Key forums 
include business planning meetings, billing issue discussions, reconciliation reviews, and order book evaluations, among others.
 T
he mechanisms in place are categorised as follows:
  C orporate-Level Engagement
 
  A
t the corporate level, there is a structured governance mechanism to capture feedback and address 
concerns through strategic and operational discussions:
 yLeadership Governance Meetings: Regular interactions with Customers’ corporate leadership teams to discuss operational performance, strategic initiatives, and alignment. These forums also serve as a platform to raise and resolve high
‑
level concerns and feedback.
 yDeployment & Planning Meetings: Engagements with central Customer teams focussing on addressing delivery
‑
related concerns, planning requirements, and resolving queries related to 
project execution.
 yBCP & Special Projects Support: Dedicated support is provided during critical situations and special initiatives to ensure seamless operations and immediate resolution of Customer concerns.
  Cir cle/ Function-level Engagement
 
  A
t the operational level, Customer issues, queries and feedback are addressed through localised and 
function
‑
specific interactions:
 yCircle Governance Meetings: Periodic reviews with circle leadership teams to assess operational performance, address escalations, and resolve region
‑
specific concerns.
 yDeployment Coordination: Continuous coordination with local teams to resolve site ‑level delivery 
is
sues and ensure timely execution.
 yOperations & Maintenance (‘O&M’) Meetings: Regular meetings to address day ‑ to ‑ day 
operational and maintenance concerns, including critical issues such as diesel management and electricity availability.
 yOperational Query Handling: Mechanisms are in place to promptly manage and resolve customer 
queries during local exigencies, ensuring minimal service disruption.
 
  T
hrough this structured governance framework and multi
‑
tier engagement model, the organisation 
ensures that Customer complaints and feedback are systematically captured, monitored, and resolved in a timely and effective manner. This proactive approach not only enhances Customer satisfaction but also drives continuous service improvement.

3.
 Mechanisms 
in place to inform Consumers of any risk of disruption/discontinuation of essential services.
 
 Ensuring 
uninterrupted passive infrastructure services is critical to our operations, and we recognise 
the importance of maintaining service continuity even during unforeseen circumstances. To address potential risks of disruption or discontinuation, we have established robust communication and contingency mechanisms.
 
 W
e proactively inform our Customers in advance of any foreseeable risks that may impact service 
availability. This includes early warnings related to natural calamities such as cyclones, storms, or extreme weather conditions, as well as situations of local unrest that could affect site accessibility or infrastructure operations. Such communication enables our customers to prepare and take necessary actions to mitigate service interruptions.
 
 In par
allel, we activate our BCPs in all such scenarios to ensure minimal disruption. This includes arranging 
alternative solutions, wherever feasible, to support continued service delivery and help Customers maintain connectivity for end users.
 
 In cases wher
e discontinuation of telecom services is unavoidable, such as due to site dismantling, a 
well
‑
defined process is followed. Customers are provided with prior intimation, allowing them sufficient 
time to reroute their services. This may be achieved through network optimisation, deployment of new sites, utilisation of alternative infrastructure, etc.
 
 T
hrough these proactive communication measures and structured processes, we strive to ensure 
transparency, minimise service disruptions, and support our Customers in maintaining seamless connectivity.

VIII. Deposits
  The Company has not accepted any deposit and as such no amount of principal or interest was outstanding as on March 31, 2026.I. Busines s Overview
  Indus Towers is a provider of tower and related infrastructure services to telecommunication service providers in India. Indus is one of the largest telecom tower companies in India basis the number of towers and co-locations operated 
by the Company. The business of 
Indus Towers is to deploy, own, operate and manage passive infrastructure pertaining to telecommunication operations. The Company provides access to its towers, primarily to wireless telecommunication service providers, on a shared basis under long-term contracts. Indus has a nationwide presence with operations in all 22 telecommunication circles in India and caters to all wireless telecommunication service providers in India.
 
 As on March 31, 2026, Indus owned and operated 264,514 
macro towers and 428,014 co-locations 
across 22 telecommunication circles. In addition, Indus owned and operated 14,044 colocations on lean towers.

II. Risk Management
  Risk management is embedded in Indus 
Towers’ operating framework. The Company strongly believes that risk resilience is key to achieving sustainable growth. The Company has a robust Risk Management Framework in place for the identification, assessment, mitigation and monitoring of key risks across the organisation. The Risk Management Framework is reviewed periodically by the Board and the Audit & Risk Management Committee, which includes discussions on Management submissions relating to risks, prioritisation of key risks and approval of action plans to mitigate such risks.
 
 The 
Company has a duly approved Risk 
Management Policy in place to support effective corporate governance and sustainable business development. The objective of this Policy is to establish a well-defined approach to risk and to set out an ongoing and consistent process for identifying, evaluating, escalating, monitoring and reporting significant risks that may be faced in the short to near term. The Policy also provides guidance on framing appropriate responses to identified key risks to ensure they are adequately addressed or mitigated.
 
 The 
Chief Risk Officer assists the Audit & Risk 
Management Committee on an independent basis by undertaking a robust review of risk assessments and associated management action plans.
 
 Operationally, risks are managed at the highest level by the Management Committee, chaired by the MD & CEO.
 
 A 
detailed discussion on Risk Management 
forms part of the Risk Management Framework Section of this Integrated Report. At present, in the opinion of the Board of Directors, there are no risks that may threaten the existence of the Company.

E P eople, Community and Sustainability
I. Human R esources
  At Indus Towers, the people strategy is a 
core pillar of sustainable value creation. During the year under review, it continued to support strong operational performance, guided by the Company’s core values and evolving business priorities, with a sustained focus on leadership strength, workforce capability and execution excellence.
 
 During 
the year, significant progress was made in 
strengthening leadership depth and succession readiness. Approximately 85% of key leadership positions were filled through internal talent, reflecting the robustness of the Company’s succession planning framework and its ability to build and retain critical capabilities internally. Organisational agility was further enhanced through large-scale talent mobility, with over 1,000 employees transitioning across roles and circles. This enabled faster deployment of talent to priority areas, improved cross-functional capability and reduced reliance on external hiring for critical roles.
 
 Focussed investments in capability building continued across levels. Over 150 high-performing
 
and high-potential Field Engineers were transitioned into specialist and critical roles, strengthening frontline effectiveness and creating a strong pipeline for technical and operational leadership.
 
 Employee engagement and development remained key priorities, supported by a strengthened rewards and recognition framework
 
and continued investments in learning and development. A blended learning ecosystem and targeted leadership programs enabled capability building at scale, aligned with both current and future business requirements. In parallel, the Company strengthened its leadership pipeline through curated in-campus programs with leading Tier 1 institutions, including Kshitij-Senior Leadership Development Program with IIM Ahmedabad, Unnati-Emerging Leader Program with IIM Lucknow, and Udaan-Young Leader Program with IIM Udaipur. These programs focussed on developing high-potential talent through structured learning, cross-functional exposure, and leadership development aligned with future capability needs. Leadership engagement was further enhanced through structured forums and Leadership Connect programs, fostering deeper engagement and effective two-way communication across the organisation.
 
 Diversity 
and inclusion continued to be a startegic 
priority with sustained progress in gender representation. Over the past three years, gender diversity has increased three-fold, from 6.3% in financial year 2022-2023 to 18.3% in financial year 2025-2026. This improvement has been driven by targeted initiatives-focussed hiring, structured learning and growth programmes such as Shakti-a leadership development program in partnership with IIM Indore; Prerna-a structured mentorship initiative; and Sangini-a community-building platform for women employees aimed at strengthening inclusion, development and retention.
 
 The 
Company remains committed to maintaining 
a safe, respectful and high-integrity workplace, supported by robust governance mechanisms and comprehensive compliance coverage across the organisation. Going forward, the Company will continue to focus on strengthening leadership pipeline depth, enhancing workforce productivity and leveraging digital and data-led HR interventions to support sustainable growth and execution excellence.
 
 A detailed discussion on Human Resource is mentioned in the Human Capital Section, which forms part of this Integrated Report.

VIII. Quality Control
  Indus Towers continues to reinforce its commitment to quality control as a strategic enabler of resilience, sustainability and long-term asset performance. Building on the strong foundation established in previous years, the Company has focussed on scale-led execution and lifecycle optimisation, ensuring that both new and ageing infrastructure deliver consistent performance in an increasingly demanding operating environment.
 
 During the year under review, a key strategic shift 
was the significant enhancement of lifecycle 
maintenance practices across the portfolio. With a nearly threefold increase in maintenance interventions, the Company proactively addressed challenges associated with ageing infrastructure. This was complemented by a substantial scale-up in tower strengthening initiatives, targeting structural degradation and ensuring long-term stability, safety and compliance with evolving engineering standards.
 
 The 
Company also recorded continued growth 
in new tower deployments, particularly in rural and hard-to-access geographies. Despite the operational complexities of such terrains, Indus Towers upheld its stringent quality benchmarks through rigorous stage-wise inspections and sustained audit programmes. This ensured that expansion into new areas did not dilute the Company’s “First Time Right” philosophy but instead reinforced execution excellence across diverse environments.
 
 Digitisation and automation emerged as key pillars of operational transformation during the year. Building on prior initiatives, the Company significantly 
expanded the integration of digital 
tools within maintenance workflows. A notable advancement was the deployment of IoT-enabled monitoring systems in diesel generators, enabling real-time performance tracking, predictive maintenance and improved fuel efficiency. This initiative aligns with the Company’s broader commitment to reducing its carbon footprint while enhancing operational reliability.

 Brief outline on CSR P
olicy of the Company:
 C orporate Social Responsibility (CSR) Policy:
  The CSR Policy of Indus Towers is aligned with the overall vision of the Company and provides a framework for 
implementing programs designed to reflect the Company’s vision and mission. As a socially responsible 
organisation, the Company believes in optimising the impact of its CSR activities.
 
 The 
CSR vision of Indus Towers aims to take an active role and responsibility in transforming the lives of 
communities by improving their socio-economic conditions. The Company has made conscious efforts to ensure that its CSR interventions are need-based, community-oriented, and sustainable, thereby creating a positive and lasting impact on the quality of life of beneficiaries as well as the broader ecosystem.
 
 The CSR Policy is formulated in accordance with the requirements of Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 
(the ‘Act’) and the Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014 (‘CSR Rules’) as amended from time to 
time. The Policy is periodically reviewed to reflect the evolving needs of communities and to incorporate amendments to the Act.
 
 The Policy encompasses the CSR vision, thematic areas of intervention, as well as the implementation, monitoring, governance, and reporting mechanisms.
 CSR Appr oach:
  Indus Towers adopts a multi-pronged approach to CSR, with a focus on delivering measurable and meaningful outcomes. The Company primarily undertakes CSR activities through its Flagship Programs – Saksham and Pragati, as detailed below:

Project Nurture: Family-Like Care Programme for Child Development
2022-23
22 States and 2 Union Territories
SoulAce
22 SOS Children’s Villages | 53 family homes | 
530 children and youthProject Period
GeographyImpact Assessment AgencyCoverage
Project Nurture was implemented by SOS 
Children’s Villages India to support parentless, abandoned and vulnerable children through the Family-Like Care (FLC) model. The programme provided residential care, education support, healthcare, nutrition services, psychosocial care, life-skills development and youth transition support across SOS Children’s Villages in India.
The programme strengthened outcomes in 
child protection, education, health, nutrition, psychosocial well-being and youth development through family-based care.Project 
Overview
The assessment found that the programme 
successfully provided safe, family-like care to all respondent beneficiaries, ensuring universal access to nutrition, healthcare, psychosocial support, and formal education. Respondent beneficiaries reported improvements in academic performance, health, confidence and emotional well-being, while 95% of respondent youth had clear educational or career aspirations. All eligible respondent youth were engaged in higher education, vocational training, internships or employment pathways. In addition, all respondent SOS Mothers participated in capacity-building programmes, strengthening the quality and consistency of family-based care.The programme strengthened holistic child development by providing a secure and nurturing family environment that enhanced children’s protection, well-being and educational outcomes. Improved access to nutrition, preventive healthcare, life skills, and learning support contributed to better physical health, academic progress and emotional resilience. The programme also strengthened youth employability and readiness for independent living through higher education, vocational training and career pathways, while enhancing caregiver capacity to deliver consistent, child-centred care and long-term developmental support.
